subject: Post-call: Pricing metrics clarification (tokens vs chars vs requests) and caching impact
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
To: Amit Shah <amit@fintechco.com>, Sophie Turner <sophie.turner@acmeretail.com>
Cc: Dev Patel <dev_patel@redwood.com>, Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-03-01T13:05:00-07:00
Subject: Thanks for the demo — quick pricing/metrics follow-up

Hi Amit / Sophie,

Thanks again for taking the time today — great discussion. Per our call, I wanted to capture the key pricing questions and proposed next steps so there's no confusion about metrics (tokens vs characters vs API requests) and how caching affects billing.

Summary from today:
- Your usage signals: ~150M characters/month across search & personalization endpoints, ~1.2M API requests/month (these are how your logs currently surface usage).
- Your budget target: you called out a target of roughly $15k–$30k/month and asked what that maps to in $/1M tokens.
- Confusion areas: 1) how characters map to tokens, 2) whether we bill per request vs per token, and 3) how prompt/response caching affects billed tokens.

Quick clarifications (short answers):
- Billing metric: Redwood bills on model tokens (input + output tokens summed) for requests that invoke the model.
- Tokens vs characters: Roughly 1 token ≈ 4 characters in English on average, but it varies by language and formatting.
- Requests vs tokens: API requests are counted for rate-limiting and throughput planning; pricing is token-based (not per request).
- Caching: If a request is served entirely from a cached response (no model call), there is no model token billing for that hit. If the runtime reuses KV/prefix state to continue generation, you’re typically billed for the tokens the model actually processed — e.g., continuing from cached state usually bills only for newly generated tokens.

Example back-of-envelope:
- 150M characters/month ≈ 37.5M tokens (150M ÷ 4).
- At a target of $18 / 1M tokens → 37.5 * $18 ≈ $675/month.
(That example assumes all chars map to billable tokens and that you have no heavy response generations — we’ll refine this with the real prompt lengths.)

Next steps I propose:
1) Can you send a CSV sample of your real traffic (a few hundred rows) with columns: timestamp, endpoint, avg_chars_in_prompt, avg_chars_in_response, request_count? I attached acme_sample_volume_breakdown.csv as a template.
2) Book a short follow-up (30–45m) with Dev (Solutions Eng) so we can run those rows through tokenization and show a cost projection and caching impact.
3) We'll also include our pricing sheet (attached) and a calculator during the call so you can play with $/1M target numbers.

If that sounds good I'll loop Dev and set up a time.

Thanks —

Hi Marissa — thanks for the recap. Helpful. A couple clarifying questions from our side:

Is the 1 token ≈ 4 characters rule robust enough for planning or do you recommend tokenizing samples?

- About caching: some of our top 20 queries are identical across users — if we cache responses at the edge, will Redwood not bill tokens for those hits? Also, what's the difference between edge response caching vs the KV/prefix cache you mentioned?

- For budget planning: if we want to target $20k/month, what's a reasonable token-volume estimate for us to provide to finance?

Happy to share a sample export — attaching an anonymized week of logs (we trimmed PII). Could you ask Dev to run it through your tokenizer so we can see realistic estimates?

Subject: Re: Thanks for the demo — quick pricing/metrics follow-up

Thanks Amit — perfect. We’ll take the sample and run a tokenization + cost projection. Some clarifications and an example so your finance team has the right context: 

1) Tokenization & accuracy: 
- The 1 token ≈ 4 characters is a rule-of-thumb for English and simple text. For planning it’s a good start, but the most accurate way is to tokenize a representative sample of your traffic (we’ll do this).

2) Edge response cache vs KV/prefix cache (how they affect billing):
- Edge response cache: this is a layer that stores full responses and serves them without calling the model. Hits served from this cache do not invoke the model and therefore do not incur token billing. Good for exact-match queries and repeated responses (e.g., top-20 queries).
- KV/prefix cache (runtime-level): this speeds up model execution by reusing internal key/value states for repeated prefixes in an ongoing session. If the runtime still needs to invoke the model to produce additional tokens, billing typically reflects the tokens the model actually processed/generated for that invocation (i.e., you generally pay for the newly processed tokens). In short: edge response cache can eliminate token billing for cache hits; KV/prefix cache reduces compute and latency and can reduce billed tokens in scenarios where only new tokens are generated.

3) Example cost scenarios (ballpark):
- Scenario A (no caching, average prompt 1,200 chars, avg response 200 chars): 
  • 1,400 chars/request ≈ 350 tokens/request (1,400 ÷ 4)
  • At 1.2M requests/month → 420M tokens/month → 420 * $18 (per 1M) ≈ $7,560/month.
- Scenario B (edge cache serves 30% of traffic entirely):
  • Billable requests drop to 0.84M month; billable tokens ≈ 294M → ≈ $5,292/month.
- Scenario C (we can reuse prefix/KV to avoid reprocessing 600 chars of prompt for 40% of traffic):
  • Effective newly billed tokens per hit drops; we'd model on your sample to quantify.

4) Budget mapping: for $20k/month at $18/1M tokens you could afford ~1.11B tokens/month (20,000 ÷ 18 ≈ 1,111 * 1M). We’ll turn your sample into a more concrete token projection so you can present a credible number to finance.

Next step: Dev can you run the attached anonymized week through our tokenizer + cost model and share a short (PDF) projection? Once we have that, we’ll schedule a 30–45m walkthrough with you and your finance lead to validate assumptions.

Thanks — looping Dev.

—Marissa
